The United Kingdom government is moving to stop schools from routinely starting General Certificate of Secondary Education (GCSE) teaching in Year 7. This, according to the government, is part of plans to overhaul the national curriculum and make the first three years of secondary education more engaging for pupils. Under the proposed changes, “schools will be expected to protect Key Stage 3 (KS3) as a distinct three-year phase, rather than using it primarily to prepare pupils for GCSE examinations.” The Department for Education announced the plans in a press release published on November 8, 2026, saying the curriculum overhaul was aimed at addressing growing disengagement among pupils in their early teenage years, as well as improving attendance and educational outcomes. The government said “some schools were increasingly encroaching on Key Stage 3 by introducing GCSE content before Year 10, with some beginning as early as Year 7.” Make PUNCH part of your everyday experience. Education Secretary, Lucy Powell, said the pressure to prepare pupils for examinations early was depriving them of a broader learning experience. “What’s more, the pressures of GCSEs and an overcrowded curriculum are resulting in too many children receiving a narrower offer during Key Stage 3 and being rushed towards exams without grasping the fundamentals or developing deeper understanding. I’m putting a stop to that,” she said. Powell said the early years of secondary education should allow children to explore different subjects, develop their interests and build a lasting enthusiasm for learning. The proposed curriculum changes will also reduce overcrowded content and improve the sequencing of subjects to allow pupils more time to develop a deeper understanding of what they are taught. The government said there would be greater emphasis on core knowledge and skills, including confident speaking, fluent reading, reading for pleasure and numeracy. Pupils would also have a more engaging offer in subjects such as drama, physical education, music and modern foreign languages, alongside technical and digital skills. According to the department, the changes are also intended to “address persistent school absence, which almost doubles between Years 7 and 9, reaching one in four children.” It said persistent absence rates among white working-class children were 75 per cent higher in secondary school than in primary school. The government said the new curriculum would discourage schools from starting GCSE specifications early for large groups of pupils or routinely requiring them to narrow their subject choices earlier or sit examinations ahead of schedule. However, teachers would retain the flexibility to stretch high-achieving pupils or groups considered ready to progress further without restricting their options. The full National Curriculum is expected to be published later in 2026, according to the release.
